title: The dynamo and the Virgin
where: *The Education of Henry Adams*, chapters 25, 19 and 1
about: Henry Adams, grandson and great-grandson of Presidents, wrote the story of his own life in 1905, at sixty-seven, and by 1907 had a hundred copies printed privately. It was published in 1918, the year he died. He tells it in the third person. The passages here come from 1900, when the scientist Samuel Langley shows him the dynamos at the Paris Exposition; from 1870, when his sister dies of lockjaw in Italy after a cab accident; and from the first page, where he is born in Boston in 1838.

view.says: Auden took the chapter’s two symbols for his own essay. For him they are two real worlds: the Dynamo’s, of masses and recurring events, told in numbers, and the Virgin’s, of faces and single events, told only in speech. Treating the first as the second is an illusion; its religion prays to the Dynamo. He says Adams took Venus and the Virgin for one person, when Venus is an impersonal force of nature in disguise.
view.quote: it was the Dynamo he worshiped, not the Virgin
view.source: “The Virgin & The Dynamo,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 61–63
view.checked: read in the scan of The Dyer's Hand, research/auden/dh.txt, lines 3095-3194; the third sentence, as the finisher reworded it, stands on p. 62, lines 3140-3143: the first of the two chimerical worlds, where the world of masses is regarded as a world of faces, and the sentence on its religion that auden[0] quotes

lenses.label: Likeness
lenses.name: simile
lenses.plain: a comparison that says one thing is like another
lenses.caption: He began to feel the dynamos as early Christians felt the Cross: one verb for both sides. Two sentences on, began to returns with no as: one began to pray. Nothing is likened now, and he has become one, the pronoun for anyone. The clause after the semicolon gives the cause, inherited instinct, and calls prayer the natural expression of man in the face of such force. The book says pray of Adams one other time: of the boy, to whom religion was not real. The religious instinct, it says there, had vanished. Auden’s verdict is that Adams worshiped the Dynamo and not the Virgin. Here Adams reports the prayer himself.
lenses.why: The simile joins machine and Cross by one verb, feel; two sentences later the likeness is gone and one, not he, begins to pray; Auden’s verdict is that Adams worshiped the Dynamo, and the passage itself reports prayer to it.

grounds.claim: the verb on both sides, the as, began to twice, he and then one, inherited instinct, man, and that the third sentence likens nothing
a simile is an explicit comparison, often but not always with like or as
grounds.source: Silva Rhetoricae (rhetoric.byu.edu), simile

lenses.label: Sentence
lenses.caption: The main clause is short: the planet seemed less impressive than this wheel. The rest hangs on it. The planet’s turning gets eight words, four of them adjectives, and the wheel gets thirty-seven. It turns within arm’s length at a dizzying speed, and three times it is said to be almost soundless: barely murmuring, scarcely humming, and it would not wake the baby that lies against it. The next sentence calls what he prays to silent and infinite force. The paragraph after says that for his purposes the dynamo’s worth was chiefly its occult mechanism, its hidden working. In electricity he saw what he saw in faith, he writes: nothing but an absolute fiat, a decree.
lenses.why: The main clause sets planet against wheel; the phrases hung on it make the wheel near, fast and almost soundless; the next sentence names it silent and infinite force, and Adams puts its value chiefly in its hidden working.

grounds.claim: the main clause; eight words and four adjectives for the planet’s turning; thirty-seven words hung on the wheel, which is near, fast and three times almost soundless
in the next sentence man prays before silent and infinite force
for his purposes the dynamo’s worth was chiefly its occult mechanism; in electricity, as in faith, all he saw was an absolute fiat
grounds.source: adams/c25, block 3

grounds.claim: occult first meant hidden or secret; fiat is the Latin for let it be done, and has meant a decree or command since 1750; vertiginous means liable to cause dizziness
grounds.source: Online Etymology Dictionary, occult (adj.), fiat (n.) and vertiginous (adj.); Merriam-Webster, vertiginous, sense 2

lenses.label: Felt

ties.say: The dynamos, and the two goddesses named together. In the next paragraph Adams calls the goddess the animated dynamo. Auden says Adams took Venus and the Virgin for one person, and that Venus is the Dynamo’s disguise.
Each is felt, and each is likened to something from the other side: the machine to the Cross, the Virgin’s force to X-rays. X-rays were named in 1895, with an *X* for the unknown.
The dynamo is prayed to. Of Venus and the Virgin, he says, no American was ever truly afraid. Later in the chapter Adams says that every known force can be measured by what it does to man.
Here the dynamo is force. In America, the other passage says, Venus and the Virgin had value at most as *sentiment*, a word that comes from the Latin verb meaning to feel.

lenses.caption: The passage under The Virgin comes six paragraphs later, and both passages use the words force and felt. Between them Adams gives his reason: he can bring such forces to one value only by how they have been felt, and he calls this translating rays into faith. The machine is likened to the Cross, and the Virgin’s force to X-rays. To the dynamo one began to pray; of Venus and the Virgin no American, he says, was ever truly afraid. Auden quoted from both in one note of 1941. For him these are two worlds, one told in numbers and one only in speech, and to treat either as the other is an illusion.
lenses.why: Adams describes the machine in words of faith and the Virgin in words of physics, and measures both by how they are felt; for Auden they are two worlds, and to take one for the other is an illusion.

grounds.claim: the words the two passages share, the two likenesses, and the two outcomes, prayer and no fear
the second passage stands in the sixth paragraph after the first

lenses.caption: The diagram follows one word through the book: force, or forces. In the twenty chapters that end in 1871, about 109,000 words, it comes 58 times. In the fifteen that begin in 1892, about 65,000 words, it comes 272 times. No chapter before this one has it more than ten times. This one has it 42 times, and says it of the dynamo and of the Virgin alike. Chapter 33 makes the word a theory of history, in which the forces of nature capture man. Force is Auden’s word too: what Adams worshiped, he says, was the Dynamo, a sign for an impersonal force of nature.

lenses.label: Who
lenses.caption: Three abstract nouns, each at the head of its sentence, are given things to do. Society can put on, Death takes features, Nature enjoys, plays, likes, smothers. The man who watches has verbs of taking in: heard, read, seen, knew, felt. He is One, then the surname Adams, then him, then one again. One is the pronoun for anyone at all, and it can stand in for I. His sister is in these lines once, as her victim, and the her is Nature’s. The paragraph before says the last lesson of his education began here. The paragraph after says such impressions are not reasoned: they are felt.
lenses.why: The abstract nouns act and the man takes in, as one or by his surname; the paragraph before says his last lesson began here, and the paragraph after says such impressions are felt, not reasoned.

grounds.claim: which nouns begin their sentences and act, which verbs the man has, what he is called, and where the sister appears

lenses.label: Pair
lenses.name: antithesis
lenses.plain: two opposed things set side by side, often in phrases of the same build
lenses.caption: Two short sentences are built on one frame: a noun, being, an adjective, a verb, and the same adjective as a noun. These two differ in their subjects, in one prefix and in their verbs: Society could put on, Adams felt only. Put on immortality is Saint Paul’s phrase, from the chapter the Book of Common Prayer reads at burials. Paul says the mortal must put it on. Adams gives it to Society, with could and at will, and leaves the mortal man only the mortality. In the next paragraph the usual remedies for pain, religion among them, become evident artifice.
lenses.why: The matched frames isolate the difference: Society can put on Saint Paul’s immortality at will, and the mortal man can only feel; the next paragraph says the usual remedies, religion among them, had become evident artifice.

grounds.claim: the two frames, part by part, and what differs between them
antithesis: contrasting words or ideas set side by side, often but not always in parallel structure
grounds.source: Silva Rhetoricae (rhetoric.byu.edu), antithesis

lenses.label: Nature
lenses.name: personification
lenses.plain: an idea or a thing spoken of in the words used for a person
lenses.caption: Nature is given a person’s verbs, enjoyed, played, liked, smothered, and a woman’s pronoun. The next paragraph says how he first came to know her attitude toward life: as a nightmare, an insanity of force. A personal God who took pleasure in such torture, it says, is unthinkable, and it ends: God could not be a Person. These lines have given Nature the pleasure that paragraph denies to God. Auden says people tend to give a face to any power they suppose is in charge of their lives. Of Adams he says that Venus is a disguise the Dynamo wears: a sign for an impersonal force of nature.
lenses.why: Nature gets a person’s verbs, a woman’s pronoun, and the pleasure in this torture that the next paragraph denies to any personal God; Auden says people tend to put faces on powers, and that Venus disguises an impersonal force.

grounds.claim: the verbs and the pronoun given to Nature, and that she likes the torture
personification: abstractions or inanimate objects referred to as having human qualities or abilities
grounds.source: Silva Rhetoricae (rhetoric.byu.edu), personification

lenses.label: Word

notes.gloss: distinctive parts · the lines of a face
notes.note: Used of the make of a body and the lines of a face since the fourteenth century, and of any distinctive part of a thing by the 1690s; from Latin *factura*, a formation, a working.

notes.gloss: power to attract · first an incantation
notes.note: In English from about 1300 for an incantation; from Latin *carmen*, a song, an enchantment. The sense of a pleasing quality came by the seventeenth century.
To kill by stopping the breath is recorded from the 1540s, to cover thickly from the 1590s.
notes.source: Online Etymology Dictionary, smother (v.); Merriam-Webster, smother

notes.gloss: a creature killed for a god
notes.note: Latin *victima*, an animal killed in sacrifice; used of a person severely hurt, tortured or killed by another from the 1650s.
Both senses of the adjective are recorded from the 1590s.

lenses.caption: Five words used of Death and Nature have a second sense on record. Features are distinctive parts, and the lines of a face. Charm was first an incantation. To smother was to kill by stopping the breath before it was to cover thickly. A victim was first a creature killed in sacrifice to a god. Winning has meant successful in a contest as long as it has meant charming. The sentence joins hard to gentle: the horror added to her charm, and the victim is smothered with caresses. In chapter 32, on the afternoon he reads of an assassination, the Virgin never looked so winning.
lenses.why: Features, charm, smother, victim and winning each have a second sense on record, and the sentence joins horror to charm and smothering to caresses; winning, said here of Nature, is said in chapter 32 of the Virgin.

grounds.claim: the senses of feature, charm, smother, victim and winning, and the dates from which each is recorded
grounds.source: Online Etymology Dictionary, feature (n.), charm (n.), smother (v.), victim (n.), winning (adj.); Merriam-Webster, smother

lenses.label: Order

spans.label: by whom and in what creed

lenses.caption: The sentence has two halves, joined at the semicolon. The subject of the first is a passage between two streets. The second begins with a house and a date, and only then, fifty-six words into the sentence, comes a child. His two verbs are passive: he was born, and was christened by an uncle. His own name is the last three words. Ten times before it a place, a man, a church or a creed is named. The next paragraph lists five of them again and calls them a nest of associations that are crowding on a ten-pound baby. It speaks of the child as branded, and of the advantage of being ticketed through life.
lenses.why: Place, church and creed fill the sentence before the child, who comes late, in the passive, his name last; the next paragraph says what the names are doing: they crowd on the baby, who is branded and ticketed through life.

grounds.claim: the order of the sentence: place first, a passage as subject, the child after fifty-six words, two passive verbs, the name last; before it ten namings of a place, a man, a church or a creed (the State House twice, the month left out)

the next paragraph lists five of the same names again among seven, says they crowd on a ten-pound baby, says he could hardly have been branded more distinctly, and speaks of the advantage of being ticketed through life
grounds.source: adams/c01, block 1

lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and a count of its words and names: the State House is counted both times it is named, and the month is not counted. [The next paragraph](#/read/adams/c01:1) in the text printed here.

lenses.label: Tense
lenses.name: correctio
lenses.plain: a correction made in the open: the writer amends a word as soon as he has used it
lenses.caption: Hancock Avenue runs, or ran. The verb is given in the present and at once amended to the past, and both are left to stand. Runs is the only present tense in the sentence: the present of the man writing, in 1905. Of the things the sentence names, the house of John Hancock had been pulled down in 1863. Hancock Avenue itself was still there in 1905. It was done away with in 1916, when the State House was extended, and when the book was published two years later only ran was true. In the next paragraph the child belongs to the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries and will have to play the twentieth century’s game.
lenses.why: The corrected verb sets the writer’s present beside 1838 and moves the place into the past; the next paragraph says the child belongs to earlier centuries; by 1918, when the book was published, the passage was gone.

grounds.claim: the present tense, the or, the past tense; runs is the one present tense in the sentence
correctio: the amending of a term or phrase just employed
grounds.source: Silva Rhetoricae (rhetoric.byu.edu), correctio

lenses.caption: The child of this sentence stays he for thirty-five chapters. In his own sentences the storyteller never writes I, me or my, and writes Henry Adams 102 times. Since Rousseau, the preface says, the self has drawn back and turned into a manikin: a tailor’s figure, there to show how the clothes of education fit. It calls the young man a certain form of energy. Twenty chapters run from 1838 to 1871, and the next begins in 1892. What a man did with his education once he had it, the book says there, is a personal matter only. In those years Adams married, and in 1885 his wife took her own life. The book tells neither.
lenses.why: The preface makes the self a manikin for showing how an education fits, and Adams is he throughout; what he did after 1871, in the years of his marriage and his wife’s death, he calls a personal matter only.

auden.says: The essay names two illusions. The aesthetic one takes the world of masses for a world of faces and makes a nature that is magical and has many gods; the sentence quoted here gives its religion. The scientific one takes the world of faces for one of masses and makes history a mechanism; its religion turns the Virgin into a statistic. Without art, he adds, there would be no idea of the sacred, and without science the gods people worship would always be false ones.
auden.quote: The aesthetic religion says prayers to the Dynamo.
auden.source: “The Virgin & The Dynamo,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), p. 62
auden.checked: read in the scan of The Dyer's Hand, research/auden/dh.txt, lines 3138-3156

auden.says: By nature, he says in the same pages, people tend to put a face on any power they imagine is responsible for their lives, and they do it to avoid responsibility: they want to say that they cannot help what they do. The pagan nature gods have masks and no real faces, because a real face answers for itself and those gods answer for nothing. Nature may rightly be given a real face, the Madonna’s for one, but only after the pagan mask is off and she is seen to be a world of masses, responsible for no one.
auden.source: “The Virgin & The Dynamo,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 62–63
auden.checked: read in the scan of The Dyer's Hand, research/auden/dh.txt, lines 3158-3180; the sentence on the Madonna runs from p. 62 to p. 63

auden.says: In his essay on American poetry Auden quotes the sentences printed here under The Virgin, with one from the paragraph before, and gives his reason for what they say. A European writer, he says, could count on a nature that had its myths, had been made human and was friendly on the whole, and on landscapes with faces a person could know and trust. The wild nature of America cannot be thought of as human or as a person. The cause, for him, was the dissenters of the Mayflower, who feared images, and also that the nature Americans had reason to fear was nothing anyone could picture as a mother.

The word *Omit* beside this book on the reading list is in an unknown hand, and it is not known whether the class read the book.

The count of *pray* is a count of the word. Adams also speaks of himself as kneeling, without that word, at the foot of the Cross in [chapter 5](#/read/adams/c05:5) and before the Virgin’s window in [chapter 32](#/read/adams/c32:15).

The counts follow the text printed here and their own rules: only *force* and *forces* are counted, a chapter’s years are those in its title, and quotation marks decide which sentences are the storyteller’s own.
The book does describe the bronze figure that Saint-Gaudens made for Adams at Rock Creek cemetery, in [chapter 21](#/read/adams/c21:24), without saying whose grave it marks.

Hancock Avenue (still there in 1903 and 1909, done away with in 1916) and the Hancock house (pulled down in 1863) now rest on Edwin M. Bacon’s guide book to Boston in three editions, read in scanned copies. No city record was seen.

The burial lesson was checked in the English Prayer Book of 1662 and in one American edition, of 1847. Whether the Adams family’s Unitarian church used that service was not looked into; the caption says only where the phrase is read.
Britannica would not open for the examiner, so nothing in the reading rests on it now; the marriage and the death rest on the Massachusetts Historical Society’s page.

The book gives its own dates in three ways: written in 1905 and privately printed in 1906 (the editor’s preface), printed in 1907 (the same preface, lower down), and the author’s preface is dated February 16, 1907. The reading follows 1905 for the writing and, since the finisher’s change, says of the hundred copies only that he had them printed by 1907.
